analysis.one_liner: Lets cities, towns, and cooperatives offer broadband even where state laws ban it.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: More than a dozen states have laws restricting cities, counties, public-private partnerships, and cooperatives from building or running their own broadband networks, often leaving residents with one expensive private provider. This bill would amend the Telecommunications Act to bar states from enforcing such bans, while requiring public networks to follow the same nondiscrimination rules as private competitors. It never moved past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities where state law blocks a public or cooperative broadband option — typically rural areas and small towns with slow, expensive, or single-provider internet service. It would also benefit local governments and co-ops that want to build networks, and it lowers prices for everyone where a public option creates competition.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents with poor or monopolized internet

how_it_helps.text: No state statute or regulation could prohibit a public provider, public-private partnership, or cooperatively organized provider from offering advanced telecommunications (broadband) service.

It defines 'public provider', 'public-private partnership provider', and 'cooperatively organized provider' (a federal-tax-law cooperative) broadly, so cities, counties, agencies, and Indian Tribes could all offer service.

It includes safeguards for competition: any public entity regulating private providers must apply its ordinances and rules without favoring its own network, and public providers stay subject to all federal and state telecom rules that apply to everyone.
The bill was written to 'preserve and protect' the ability of states, localities, partnerships, and co-ops to provide broadband — a direct counter to state-level bans on community networks.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent cable and telephone companies would face new competition in markets where they currently hold a state-protected monopoly, and taxpayers in a community that builds a network bear the financial risk if the project fails or costs overrun.

drawbacks.text: Public broadband networks are built with public money, so a failed or over-budget municipal project would fall on local taxpayers rather than shareholders.
The bill preempts state law nationwide, overriding states' own judgments about whether municipal entry is prudent — a genuine federalism concern a good-faith opponent would raise.
The bill only removes bans; it does not fund networks, so communities still need to find financing, and savings depend on whether public options actually materialize.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For communities stuck with one overpriced provider, the upside is real: competition tends to lower prices and improve service, and the bill's antidiscrimination and level-playing-field provisions address the strongest objection (that city-owned networks would get favorable regulatory treatment). The risks are localized — a losing bet costs that town's taxpayers, not the public at large.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology subcommittee, where it sat without a markup or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the Community Broadband Act of 2023 on April 10, 2023, with eight original cosponsors including Rep. James Clyburn.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on April 21 to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology.
Twenty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
No further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever taken, and the bill died with the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent broadband providers keep the state-level bans on community networks they backed, and the residents who could have gained a cheaper public option keep waiting. No one who supports local broadband options is better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent broadband providers and state restriction laws

for.name: Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; it sat in the Communications and Technology subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill beyond referring it to a subcommittee; no markup or vote was ever held.

against.name: Incumbent cable and telecom providers
against.what_they_did: Industry groups have long supported state laws that restrict municipal broadband, the restrictions this bill would void.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled committee.

industries.industry: Incumbent cable and telephone broadband providers
industries.note: State laws banning or restricting municipal and cooperative broadband shield these incumbents from local competition, letting them charge more with no cheaper alternative. By voiding those state bans, the bill would expose them to competition, which typically lowers prices and improves service for residents.

industries.industry: Municipal governments, public utilities, and broadband cooperatives
industries.note: These entities could offer broadband wherever state law currently forbids it. Their gains come from expanding affordable access rather than from charging more, though they would also carry the financial risk of building networks.
